e7440fe548.q: What framework should leaders use to set up effective mentoring relationships from the first meeting?
e7440fe548.a: Eric Dillon emphasizes establishing clear structure from the initial conversation: addressing confidentiality expectations, defining specific mentoring goals, ensuring transparency with the mentee's direct leader, agreeing on meeting cadence and agenda responsibility, scheduling a feedback check-in after a couple of meetings to assess fit, and conducting a final assessment to evaluate success. He found that getting these structural elements clear early allows mentors and mentees to reach substantive conversations much faster and harvest significantly more learnings.
e7440fe548.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

45e6744594.q: How can leaders build the next generation through scaled mentoring while maintaining quality and personal investment?
45e6744594.a: Dillon maintains a detailed scorecard tracking over 122 mentoring relationships, recording the nature of each relationship, mentoring goals, and success outcomes. He has learned to identify areas where he adds the most value and to refer mentees to other mentors in his network when a better fit exists. By passing his mentorship question to 122 people behind him, he has created a multiplier effect where those mentees now maintain their own mentoring scorecards and continue the cycle of capacity building.
45e6744594.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

3bb36b537f.q: Why should confidentiality be a two-way commitment in mentor-mentee relationships?
3bb36b537f.a: Confidentiality works both directions: the mentee protects information shared by the mentor, and the mentor protects sensitive details shared by the mentee. Dillon shares real-world scenarios, board packages, and live case studies as teaching tools—information that requires mutual trust. He vets candidates carefully, conducts preliminary meetings before engaging, and has an agreement he can deploy if necessary, viewing it more as reinforcement of commitment than legal enforcement.
3bb36b537f.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

d65457a412.q: What is the primary responsibility of business leaders in modern organizations?
d65457a412.a: According to Dillon, the primary job of leaders is to build more leaders—before celebrating business success or annual results. He emphasizes that in organizations today, human potential is the capital that matters most, and leaders must create environments where employees choose to return to work, invest in their development, and set them up for success whether they stay or eventually leave.
d65457a412.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

c21dd5a5ff.q: How should leaders approach candid feedback and transparency in mentoring relationships?
c21dd5a5ff.a: Dillon was more hesitant about directness in his early mentoring years but became increasingly courageous and unapologetic about it. He now matter-of-factly tells mentees to own their development, be transparent with their leaders about mentoring relationships, and discuss why, where, how, and with whom they are pursuing development. This transparency can sometimes ignite interest from the mentee's direct leader and create a more productive relationship overall.
c21dd5a5ff.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

ad7160813e.q: How has the nature of business capital changed in financial services, and what does this mean for leadership?
ad7160813e.a: Historically, capital in banking meant money locked in vaults to build plants and create economic goodwill. Today, Dillon argues, organizational capital is largely human potential—and employees go home every night. Leaders must create environments where people choose to return to work, invest in their futures, and set them up for success. In finance, this shift is more pronounced than ever, as the industry increasingly depends on knowledge workers rather than repeatable tasks.
ad7160813e.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

e84d903cbc.q: What role might artificial intelligence play in the future of leadership and human capability?
e84d903cbc.a: While some argue AI will diminish the importance of people, Dillon believes it will accelerate the need for human judgment and leadership. As AI and tools handle easier repeatable tasks, the ability to exercise judgment, have courageous conversations, and harvest diversity become even more critical—capabilities that tools cannot yet replicate.
e84d903cbc.e: How To Be An Effective Mentor Who Builds The Next Generation Of Leaders - Winning with Eric Dillon, President of General Bank of Canada

a75a7043e6.q: How should organizations handle talented employees who seek opportunities the company cannot provide?
a75a7043e6.a: Rather than holding employees back, Dillon advocates setting them up for success and allowing them to move on if the organization lacks the opportunity they are passionate about. Good things happen to good people, and employees who leave well-equipped may return three years later as much more capable and better-equipped professionals for challenges the organization faces at that time.
